name: LavinMQ
workload: Field-staff messaging platform (WhatsApp/Telegram/WeChat integration for a waste-management workforce of 16,000+) migrated from a Kafka integration to LavinMQ via Broadway consumers.
claimed_speedup: Memory usage dropped from 5 GB to under 40 MB in a development instance; message-consuming times decreased 3x, message-publishing times improved 300x versus the prior Kafka integration; daily message volume grew from ~4,000 to 50,000+ after migration
tradeoffs: AMQP 0-9-1/MQTT semantics differ from Kafka's log-based model (no offset replay, different consumer-group semantics); numbers come from one customer's migration writeup, not a controlled apples-to-apples benchmark; the prior Kafka deployment's sizing/tuning is unstated.
caveats: First-party case-study blog post (customer testimonial via CloudAMQP's own site), no stated hardware/instance sizing for either side, no independent reproduction; the memory figure is explicitly 'in a development' environment, not production.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos topic:message-broker --sort stars, then WebFetch of lavinmq.com blog case study linked from the lavinmq.com homepage

name: RabbitMQ
workload: One publisher + one consumer, Kafka (confluent-kafka/librdkafka client) and RabbitMQ (pika blocking client) both containerized on the same host, 4 CPU/4GB each, 4 lanes, 256-byte payloads, durability level 'broker' (Kafka acks=1 / RabbitMQ persistent+publisher-confirms), end-to-end publish-to-consume latency at an offered rate of 500 msg/s where both brokers keep up.
claimed_speedup: RabbitMQ p50 2.6ms vs Kafka p50 6.5ms at 500 msg/s (~2.5x lower median latency); tails converge at p99.9 (RabbitMQ 11.1ms vs Kafka 11.0ms, effectively tied) (derived from page data for the ratio)
hardware: Apple Silicon laptop, Docker Desktop, both brokers containerized with identical 4 CPU / 4GB limits sharing the host with the load generator; exact chip model (M1/M2/M3/etc.) not stated
tradeoffs: RabbitMQ loses badly on fan-out in the same suite (22,000 vs Kafka's 176,000 messages retained for 8 readers) and reorders 11.5% of same-key messages at 8 consumers vs 0% for Kafka; RabbitMQ's confirmed-publish throughput here is capped by pika's lack of batched confirms (one round trip per message), so above ~1,100 msg/s the 'RabbitMQ' numbers actually measure the load generator's backlog, not the broker.
caveats: Single laptop, single node each, RF=1/no replication tested, results are as much about client-library choice (librdkafka vs pika) as about the brokers themselves; exact CPU model not given; the benchmark repo itself has 0 stars and is a personal project, though its methodology (repeated runs, a documented coordinated-omission fix, committed raw JSON results) is unusually rigorous.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "kafka vs" benchmark --sort updated

name: NATS JetStream
workload: Single-node docker-compose deployment (Kafka in KRaft mode vs NATS with JetStream enabled), single partition/stream, small JSON payloads, steady-state mode: producer paced at 500 msg/s, consumer already tailing, 5s warm-up + 20s measurement window, native Go clients (franz-go for Kafka, nats.go JetStream client for NATS), latency measured with HdrHistogram.
claimed_speedup: p50 0.5ms vs Kafka's 7.2-7.8ms (~14-15x), p99 0.9ms vs 12.7-13.5ms (~14x), p999 2.8ms vs 14.0-19.1ms (~5-7x) (derived from page data)
tradeoffs: Single-broker, no replication, no consumer-group/partition parallelism exercised; author explicitly cautions that this single-core, low-concurrency setup doesn't exercise thread-per-core designs and shouldn't be read as a general ranking; JetStream lacks Kafka's log-compaction/Kafka-Streams/Connect/schema-registry ecosystem.
caveats: Benchmark repo has 0 stars, no CPU model stated, single run; the same repo's burst-mode latency numbers are called 'not meaningful' by its own author (only the steady-state numbers, used here, are presented as trustworthy); not independently reproduced elsewhere in this search.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "kafka vs" benchmark --sort updated

name: StrikeMQ
workload: Internal micro-benchmarks (benchmarks/ dir, strikemq_bench binary) of a single-node, Kafka-wire-compatible broker: 1KB log append, SPSC ring push+pop, and Kafka protocol header decode.
claimed_speedup: Log append 1KB: 83ns p50 / 4.4us p99.9; SPSC ring push+pop 42ns p99.9; Kafka header decode 42ns p99.9; broker startup <10ms and 0% idle CPU, contrasted with Kafka's JVM/ZooKeeper cold start; no direct side-by-side number against a running Kafka instance is given on the page
tradeoffs: Explicitly positioned as a dev/test stand-in ('like LocalStack for AWS'), not for production load; single-node only, no replication or consumer-group durability guarantees comparable to real Kafka; only latency/micro-op numbers are published, no throughput numbers.
caveats: Numbers are self-reported micro-benchmarks of internal components (log append, ring buffer, header decode) rather than a measured comparison against a running Kafka broker on shared hardware; small hobby project (14 stars), no stated compiler/CPU for the benchmark run.

name: Monocoque
workload: REQ/REP round trip over TCP (per-run network namespace) and IPC (Unix domain socket), payload sizes 16B-16KiB, one socket pair per run, libzmq 4.3.5 vs monocoque 0.4.1 (default compio/io_uring backend, plus tokio and smol backends), 5 replicates per cell with outlier detection, each implementation built in a pinned Docker image and executed directly on bare metal (chroot + network namespace, no container runtime) under zmq-arena's harness.
claimed_speedup: p50 latency 2.75x-3.12x faster than libzmq across IPC and TCP at 64B/1024B/16384B payloads (e.g. IPC 1024B: monocoque 13.79us vs libzmq 42.16us p50, 16.80us vs 47.49us p99); monocoque's tokio backend goes further, ~3-4x at small IPC payloads (derived from page data)
hardware: 13th Gen Intel Core i5-13400 (16 threads), Ubuntu 24.04.2 LTS, kernel 6.8.0-58-generic, x86_64, performance governor, turbo disabled, bare metal, run as root (per the run's recorded hardware block)
tradeoffs: Benchmark is authored by the same person who wrote both monocoque and the zmq-arena harness (first-party, though code, hardware and raw per-cell JSON are all public and independently re-runnable); monocoque is a from-scratch ZMTP 3.1 reimplementation rather than a libzmq wrapper, so it forgoes libzmq's mature C ABI, CURVE hardening track record, and broad language-binding ecosystem; each engine is built from a version-pinned Docker image (image digest recorded) rather than a bare compiler-flags string.
caveats: Single machine, single socket pair (no fan-out or multi-peer contention) REQ/REP workload only; only two historical runs published (2026-08-21, 2026-08-26) and no independent third party has reproduced the result yet; repo still small (46 stars).
